pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: This page explains, in ten minutes, how the shop's work flows through this workspace. Read it once, then share it with the dispatcher and each plumber.
What lives where
Customers

: every home, landlord, restaurant and property manager you serve, with where the main shutoff is, how old their water heater is, and whether they are on a maintenance plan. Each card adds up what you have billed them, what they still owe, and how many jobs are open.
Jobs
: every call, from a running toilet to a two-bath rough-in. A job carries the plumber, the date, the price, parts and labor cost, and the margin.
Parts and van stock
: what is on each van and on the shop shelf, its cost, and when it needs reordering.
Invoices
: what you billed, what has been paid, and what is late.
A job from first call to paid
The call comes in. The dispatcher adds a job on the Jobs board (or the customer uses the Request a job form) and it lands as
New request
The dispatcher picks the lead plumber, sets the date and moves it to
Scheduled
. The plumber can press
Assign to me
to take it, and it then shows in their own Mine list.
On the day, the plumber opens the job sheet, works the checklist, and enters parts cost and hours before leaving.
Mark done
closes the job and stamps today's date.
The office raises the invoice and sets it to
Sent
. If the due date passes, set it to
Overdue
. The customer's
Awaiting payment
counts both, so nothing late hides.
When money arrives,
Mark paid
stamps the date.
Your weekly rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard. Clear overdue jobs first, then call anyone on the Awaiting payment list who is past due
Every afternoon: check tomorrow on the Jobs calendar and confirm with customers
Every Friday: van restock, see the restock page
Every month: look at Callbacks and Thin margins with the team
Making it yours
Change the work types, priorities and neighborhoods to match your area. Add your real vans in
Kept on
. Delete the sample customers once you have entered ten of your own. Nothing here needs special setup: type into any cell, drag cards between columns, and every total updates by itself.
The three numbers that run a plumbing shop: jobs still open, money still owed (sent and overdue invoices together), and callbacks, the return trips you do not get paid for.
Overdue jobs
My jobs
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Callbacks
Water damage grows by the hour, and so does the customer's panic. A calm, complete first call saves the house and wins a customer for twenty years.
The first two minutes on the phone

Ask if anyone is hurt and whether water is near outlets, a panel or light fixtures. If yes, tell them to stay out of that room and to shut the breaker only if they can reach the panel from a dry floor.
Get them to the main shutoff. Look up the customer: if they are already in Customers, read them the
Main shutoff location
you saved last time. If not, the usual spots are the basement wall facing the street, a crawlspace near the front, a garage wall, or the meter box at the curb.
If the leak is on the hot side only, the valve on the cold inlet at the top of the water heater will stop it without shutting off the whole house.
Get the address, a callback number, gate or lockbox codes, and ask for two photos by text: the leak and the area under it.
Tell them what happens next and when. Never promise an arrival time you cannot keep.
Dispatch
Add the call on the Jobs board as New request with priority
Emergency
, then set Scheduled for today.
Pick the plumber, not the van: the nearest person who can solder copper and crimp PEX, with a dry-vac and a moisture meter on board.
Text the customer the plumber's name and a 30-minute window. If the window slips, the dispatcher calls, not the plumber.
If a second emergency lands, move the routine job, never the emergency. Call that routine customer yourself to rebook.
On site
Water off and confirmed off at a fixture
Photos before any wall or ceiling is opened
Moisture readings written on the job sheet
Temporary repair or permanent repair agreed with the customer, with the price, before work starts
Old pipe kept for the customer if they want to show their insurer
Example: a split line in a crawlspace

A customer calls at 6:40 on a January morning: water in the basement, no idea where it comes from. The dispatcher talks her to the shutoff in the crawlspace hatch, books Keisha for 7:30, and texts the window. Keisha finds a frozen split on the cold line, replaces two feet with PEX and a pair of couplings, and insulates the run. Parts were under a hundred dollars; the job was four hours with drying. The invoice goes out from the van before she leaves.
After the visit

If the damage is large, tell the customer to call their insurer and give them a written list of what was found and what was replaced. Do not guess what their policy covers. Note the cause on the job so the next plumber knows the history of that house. If the same leak brings you back within thirty days, tick
Callback
on the new job: the Dashboard counts them, and a rising count usually points to a training or parts problem, not bad luck.

A standard tank swap is a half-day job that goes wrong in the same three places: the wrong size heater on the van, no permit, and venting or gas lines that are not to code. Sort all three before the day.
Before the day
Look up the house in Customers.
Water heater installed (year)
tells you the age; most tanks give out between 8 and 12 years.
Confirm fuel (gas or electric), capacity, height, and venting. A photo of the data plate answers most of it.
Check the permit. In most places a replacement needs one. Set
Permit
on the job to Applied the day you file, and to Approved when it comes back.
Reserve the heater. Parts shows how many are on the shelf; if the count is at or under the reorder point, call the supplier the same day.
Load the van: expansion tank, gas flex connector, dielectric unions, a new drain pan, seismic straps where they are required, and a dolly.
On the day
Shut off gas or the breaker, then the cold supply
Drain the old tank to the floor drain or outside, never into the yard next to the foundation
Set the new tank in a pan, strap it, and connect water lines with unions
Fit or replace the expansion tank and check the pressure matches the house pressure
Gas: leak-test every joint with solution. Electric: fill the tank completely before power is turned back on
Check the draft hood or the power vent, then the relief valve discharge line runs down to within six inches of the floor
Run a hot tap until the water is hot, and show the customer the temperature setting
Pricing it
Price the swap as one flat amount the customer can say yes to: heater, standard parts, haul-away, permit and labor. Put the real parts cost and hours on the job so the
Margin

column tells the truth. A good swap should leave at least thirty percent margin; the Margin check marks anything under twenty percent as Thin. Add-ons such as a new gas shutoff, an expansion tank or a code-required pan are quoted separately and written on the job sheet.
Example

A family's 50-gallon gas tank fails at eleven years with rust at the base. The office quotes a flat price on the phone from the data-plate photo, files the permit that afternoon, and Bram swaps it the next morning in five and a half hours. Parts were about half the price; margin lands above forty percent. After the inspection passes, the office sets Permit to Inspected and offers the yearly
Water heater flush
plan, which shows on the customer's card from then on.
After the swap
Update the customer's water heater year so the next call starts with the right facts.
Book the inspection and be there for it if the inspector asks.
Haul the old tank to the recycler; scrap steel often pays for the trip.
A plumber who drives to the supply house in the middle of the day loses an hour of billable time and often the next job. Ten minutes on Friday afternoon fixes that.
Every Friday, before the vans go home
Each plumber opens Parts, filters to their own van with
Kept on
, and counts the bins. Type the real count over the old one and set Last counted to the day.
Anything that shows
Reorder
goes on one order per supplier. The office sends the orders before 4 pm so they are on the will-call shelf by 7 am Monday.
Shop-shelf items, such as water heaters and expansion tanks, are counted by the office. Never let water heaters drop below two: they are the jobs that pay for the week.
What every van carries
Toilet: wax rings, fill valves, flappers, closet bolts, a flange repair ring
Water: 1/2 and 3/4 in copper and PEX fittings, push couplings, ball valves, supply lines in three lengths
Drain: a hand auger and a 50 ft cable machine, trap kits, test balls
Consumables: thread tape, pipe dope, flux, solder, shop rags, floor covers and shoe covers
Safety: gas leak detector, moisture meter, a first aid kit and a fire extinguisher
Setting reorder points

Start with how many you use in two weeks, then add what one bad day eats. If you use six fill valves a fortnight and a big apartment call can use four, set the reorder point at ten. Review the points every quarter: the Stock value column shows how much money is sitting on shelves, and a shelf full of slow parts is cash you cannot spend.
When something runs out on a job
Tell the dispatcher before leaving the job
Check whether another van has it nearby before driving to the supplier
Write the part on the job so its cost lands in the margin
Raise the reorder point if it happens twice in a month
Example

On Friday Keisha counts Van 2 and finds six push couplings against a reorder point of ten. The row shows Reorder, and the office adds a box to the Inland Pipe order. On Monday a burst pipe call needs four; she has them, and the job is done in one trip.
